Let’s dive into Chapter 1: Facing the Questions We’re Not Supposed to Ask.
Have you ever noticed how the air in a room seems to change when someone mentions death? Most people—whether they’re at a family dinner or just chatting with friends—tend to steer the conversation away. But deep down, we’re all curious about what comes after life ends. In fact, kids are usually the ones brave enough to ask out loud. They go straight for the big mysteries: What really happens to a body after death? Why do we have the rituals we do? And—maybe you’ve heard this one—will a pet ever turn on its owner after they die?
In our world, death is something we keep hidden, wrapped in gentle words and closed doors. But for a mortician, it’s part of everyday life—dealing with the realities that most people never see. It’s often kids who ask the most honest, sometimes even poetic, questions. They want to know if a body can explode, if a head could ever be put back on, or if a corpse might suddenly sit up. Grown-ups usually laugh nervously or try to change the subject, but really, these questions come from a place of wanting to understand what nobody talks about.
I remember one afternoon when a group of school kids visited a funeral home on a field trip. Their teacher looked a bit on edge, hoping they’d stay quiet and respectful. But as soon as the mortician started talking, hands shot up everywhere. One kid asked, “What happens if you die on an airplane?” Another wanted to know, “Can you keep your grandma’s skull?” The mortician handled it all with a mix of science and gentle humor, and the kids listened—absolutely captivated—as the mysteries of death started to feel a little less scary.
And you know what? The more openly these questions were answered, the less power fear had over them. Even adults, once they realized it was okay, admitted they had their own secret questions—about what really happens to a body, or why we grieve the way we do. A lot of folks have been carrying these curiosities for years, not sure if it’s okay to ask.
Here’s something to remember: death is both a biological fact and a cultural experience. The body changes in predictable ways—some are dramatic, some are subtle, all guided by nature. But how we react to death, the rituals we follow, and the ways we remember someone? That’s different for every family, every culture, every time in history. And when we don’t talk about it openly, myths and misunderstandings tend to grow.
In the mortuary, science and personal experience blend together. Families might quietly wonder if their loved one will look peaceful, or if a body can move after death. The real answers are often less frightening than our imaginations make them out to be. Most of our fears are born from not knowing—and the unknown isn’t usually as dramatic as we think.
So, by making space for any question—no matter how odd or uncomfortable—death becomes something we can face with curiosity rather than fear. The mortician’s job isn’t just looking after those who’ve passed; it’s about helping the living find answers, and maybe a little peace. When we start having these honest conversations, the taboo around death begins to fade. What’s left is a sense of shared understanding and humanity.
